result.title: Tradeoffs between objective outcomes and human enjoyment of work in human-AI task allocation
result.summary: For people, tasks at work are defined by more than their outcome: they are colored by the experience of engaging in that task. As AI systems become increasingly capable of performing human-level work they may be deployed to tasks that people find enjoyable while simultaneously creating comparatively more aversive tasks such as monitoring AI outputs. This creates a thorny tradeoff for managers: whether work should be assigned purely based on the expected performance of the workers in question, or also account for the subjective experience of the person potentially doing the task. Most economic accounts focus on expected utility calculations based on the former. Here, we assess how people balance objective outcomes and more subjective qualities like enjoyment. In a series of large-scale (N=800) behavioral studies in which people allocate tasks to either an AI or human worker we find that people's allocation decisions are best captured by a model that systematically balances relative objective performance with the human worker's expected enjoyment, weighting human experience higher when a task is framed as inducing less enjoyment and adjusting based on the stakes of the task. As AI also makes decisions about work allocation, we compare a set of LLMs. We find many models also deviate from purely objective decisions, particularly when the project stakes are low, but there is wide heterogeneity as to how much and in what manner they weigh enjoyment. These results raise questions about what role human experience may play in decisions around where and how to integrate AI into workplaces. Integration may be jagged across settings due to consideration not only of the relative capabilities of workers, but also the human experience of work, the valence of that experience (e.g., more strongly weighing aversion), the context (e.g., stakes), and who is making or guiding such choices (human or LLM).
